transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess the short version is that I’m not feeling quite like myself lately. I’m an elementary—well, middle school now—teacher, and the district recently put this bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on me on top of my regular teaching responsibilities. And I can do it, technically, I mean I’m still showing up and getting through the school day, but it’s been sitting on me in a way I didn’t expect.

I feel wound up a lot, and discouraged, which is not really how I usually am about work. I’ve always been the kind of person who handles lesson plans and emails and all the little follow-up things pretty automatically, but lately I keep putting them off. I’ll look at my inbox or know I need to adjust a lesson plan, and I just sort of avoid it, which is frustrating because that’s not like me. So I came in because I don’t want it to keep getting worse, and I’m trying to understand what’s going on.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about things, even when there isn’t a clear reason, or feeling like you can’t quite control your anxiety?

I wouldn’t say it comes completely out of nowhere, if that’s what you mean. It feels pretty tied to this work situation—ever since the district added this bilingual social-emotional learning rollout onto my regular teaching load. I’m still functioning, I’m still going in and teaching and getting through the day, but I feel wound up in a way that doesn’t feel like me.

And it’s discouraging, honestly, because I’m used to being pretty steady with work things. Lesson plans, emails, all the little follow-up pieces—I’ve handled those for years without making a big production of it. Lately I’ll know I need to sit down and revise something or respond to messages, and I just put it off. Then I feel worse because I’m not used to avoiding those things. So the anxiety is there, yes, but it feels like it’s wrapped around this added responsibility more than just random worrying for no reason.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms, like restlessness, fatigue, or muscle tension, especially when you're thinking about these work responsibilities?

I mean, the main thing I notice is feeling wound up, yes, especially when I’m thinking about that rollout or all the pieces attached to it. It’s not like I’m falling apart during the school day—I’m still there, still teaching, still doing what has to be done in front of the students—but inside I feel tense and kind of discouraged in a way that really doesn’t feel like me.

It’s mostly tied to the extra responsibility the district put on me, the bilingual social-emotional learning program on top of my regular teaching. I’ll think, okay, I need to adjust these lesson plans, I need to answer those emails, I need to stay on top of the rollout materials, and instead of just doing it like I normally would, I put it off. And then that makes me feel even more wound up, because I’m used to handling those things without a second thought. So yes, physically or emotionally—maybe both—I feel keyed up around it, even though I can still get through the day.
Outside of work, do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried about other areas of your life, like relationships, health, or everyday responsibilities?

Not really in the same way, no. I mean, of course I have ordinary life things I think about, like anyone does, but what brought me in is very specifically this work situation. Ever since the district put this bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate, on top of my regular teaching, it’s like I can still get through the school day and do what I need to do in front of the students, but I feel wound up and discouraged in a way that just doesn’t feel like me.

Outside of work, it’s more that the work feeling follows me home, if that makes sense. I’ll be thinking about lesson plans I haven’t adjusted or emails I haven’t answered, and those are things I used to handle almost automatically. Now I catch myself putting them off, and then I feel worse because I know I’m avoiding them. But I wouldn’t say I’m suddenly anxious about my relationships or my health or every little everyday responsibility. It’s really centered around this added responsibility at school.
Have you noticed that you’re not getting the same satisfaction or enjoyment out of things you usually like to do, even outside of work?

I’m not sure I’d say I’ve lost enjoyment in things, exactly. I mean, I haven’t sat down and thought, “Oh, I don’t like this anymore,” if that’s what you mean. It’s more that when I’m outside of work, I’m often still sort of mentally tangled up in the work piece, so I may not settle into things as easily.

But I wouldn’t want to overstate it. If I’m doing something I usually enjoy, I can still enjoy it. It’s just that sometimes there’s this background noise in my head about what I haven’t finished or what I need to respond to, and that makes it harder to feel fully relaxed. So… not no enjoyment, really. More like my attention gets pulled back toward school.
Have you noticed feeling down or losing interest in things more often, even small things that used to feel rewarding or give you a sense of accomplishment?

I wouldn’t say it’s like I’ve lost interest across the board, but yes, I do feel more discouraged than I’m used to, and it’s mostly around this work situation. I came in because ever since the district put this bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate—on top of my regular teaching—I can still get through the day and do what I need to do, but I feel wound up and discouraged in a way that just isn’t like me.

And the part that bothers me is that small work things that used to give me a sense of, “Okay, that’s done, I’m on top of it,” don’t feel that way right now because I’m putting them off. Lesson plans, emails, rollout materials—those are things I used to handle without a second thought. Now I’ll know I need to do them, and I’ll avoid them, and then I feel worse because that’s not how I usually operate. So it’s not that nothing feels rewarding anymore, exactly. It’s more that this added responsibility has made me feel kind of stuck and discouraged, and even little accomplishments at work don’t come as naturally as they used to.
Have you noticed feeling down or in a low mood most of the time, even when you're not thinking about work?

Not most of the time, no. I mean, I do feel discouraged, and more than I’m used to, but when I really look at it, it keeps circling back to the school situation. Ever since the district put this bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate on top of my regular teaching, I can still get through the day and be present for the students, but I feel wound up and kind of defeated in a way that doesn’t feel like me.

When I’m not thinking about work, I don’t think I’m just sitting in a low mood all the time. It’s more like work intrudes. I’ll be at home and suddenly remember lesson plans I haven’t adjusted, or emails I haven’t answered, and then I get that heavy, discouraged feeling because those are things I used to handle without much thought. Now I’m putting them off, and that makes me feel worse about myself.

So I wouldn’t say I’m low even completely separate from work. It’s more that this work stress has started spilling over, and I’m having trouble shaking it off.
Have you found it hard to control your worry, even when you try, or noticed that it’s starting to interfere with your ability to focus or get things done outside of work?

Yes… I think that’s the part I’m having the hardest time admitting, honestly. I’m still functioning. I’m still showing up, still teaching, still doing the day-to-day things I absolutely have to do. So from the outside, I probably look like I’m managing.

But I’m not managing the way I normally do. I’ve pushed back planning deadlines, or just sort of missed the internal deadlines I would usually set for myself. And there have been a few times where colleagues have had to remind me about things—small tasks, planning pieces, materials, follow-ups—that I used to just take care of reliably. That feels very unlike me.

It’s not that I’m completely unable to work or anything like that. It’s more that the worry keeps taking up space in my head, and then I’ll avoid starting something, or I’ll jump between things and not finish them. Then someone checks in or reminds me, and I feel embarrassed because I’m usually the person who has those things handled. So yes, it has started interfering, even if I’m still keeping the basic responsibilities going.
Have you found that activities you usually enjoy don’t feel rewarding or pleasurable anymore, even when you're not thinking about work?

I don’t think so… not in that broad way you’re asking. I mean, I have moments where I’m distracted, so something I’d normally enjoy might not fully land because my mind drifts back to school. But I wouldn’t say pleasure is gone from things in general.

If I’m really not thinking about work, I can still enjoy things. It’s more that getting myself fully away from thinking about work has been harder. So the activity itself isn’t the problem, if that makes sense. It’s not like I sit down to do something I normally like and feel absolutely nothing. It’s more that I’ll be trying to relax and then a thought about some task or email or planning piece pops in, and it sort of interrupts the enjoyment.

So no, I haven’t noticed that everything outside of work feels unrewarding. It’s more tied to whether I can actually get my head out of work mode.
Have you noticed a lasting loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, even when you're not thinking about work?

I don’t think I’d call it a lasting loss, no. At least, not the way I understand what you’re asking. I still do have interest in things I normally enjoy, and if I’m actually able to be present with them, they can still feel good.

It’s more that my attention gets pulled away, if that makes sense. Like I might start doing something I usually like and then I realize I’m half there, half somewhere else mentally. But it doesn’t feel like the enjoyment itself is gone. It feels more like I’m not always giving myself enough mental space to enjoy it.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed a steady, across-the-board loss of interest or pleasure when work isn’t on my mind. If I’m truly not thinking about work, I can still enjoy things.
Have you noticed feeling down or in a low mood even when you’re not thinking about work or any of the added responsibilities at school?

I wouldn’t say I feel low in a completely separate, out-of-nowhere way. It feels tied to all of this school responsibility, even when I’m not actively sitting there thinking, “Oh, the rollout, the emails, the lesson plans.” It’s like the pressure has followed me around.

Ever since the district put that bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate, on top of my regular teaching, I’ve felt… wound up, and honestly pretty discouraged in a way that doesn’t feel like me. I still get through the day. I’m not falling apart in front of my class or anything. But there’s this heaviness or discouragement that’s been there because I know I’m not keeping up the way I usually do.

And then I’ll put off things like lesson plans or emails—things I used to just handle without a second thought—and that makes me feel worse about myself. So yes, I guess I do feel down at times, but I see it as connected to this added responsibility and the stress around school, not like a general low mood that’s totally unrelated to it.
Have you found that you’ve lost interest in almost all activities, even ones you used to enjoy, even temporarily?

No, I don’t think I’ve lost interest in almost all activities. Even temporarily, I’m not sure I’d describe it that strongly.

There are times when I sort of don’t feel like doing much, but when I really think about it, it’s usually because I’m preoccupied or tired from having my mind on school things. It’s not that the activities themselves suddenly seem meaningless or like I don’t care about them anymore. If I can settle into something, I can still enjoy it.

So… I guess my answer is no, not almost all activities. It’s more like my attention gets hijacked, rather than my interest disappearing.
Have you noticed that even when you’re not thinking about work, things you used to enjoy feel less satisfying or take more effort to get into?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed that in the way you mean. I mean, I can think of moments where something takes me longer to settle into, but I don’t know that it’s because the thing itself feels less satisfying. It’s more like I’m a little… distracted or not fully shifted out of “school mode,” even if I’m not consciously thinking through work.

Like, if I sit down to do something I normally like, I might need a few minutes to actually feel present. But once I’m there, it can still feel enjoyable. So I wouldn’t say the enjoyment is gone or that things consistently feel dull or empty. It’s more that I don’t always transition into them as easily right now.

So, I guess my answer is: not really less satisfying, no. Maybe sometimes a little more effort to get into, but not because I’ve stopped caring about them.
Have you noticed any days where you feel like nothing gives you pleasure or interest, even things you normally enjoy, and this lasts for most of the day, even when work isn’t on your mind?

No, I don’t think so. Not in that “nothing gives me pleasure” kind of way, and not for most of a day.

I mean, there are stretches where I’m kind of dulled out or I’m not as quick to reach for something enjoyable, if that makes sense. Like I might not immediately think, “Oh, I want to do this nice thing,” because my mind feels crowded or I’m just not very settled. But if I’m actually doing something I normally like, I can still get something out of it. It may take me a little while to shift gears, but I wouldn’t say the pleasure is absent.

So… no, I haven’t noticed whole days where everything feels pointless or flat even when work isn’t on my mind. It’s more uneven than that, and it still feels connected to being distracted or weighed down by the school situation rather than losing interest in life in general.
Outside of thinking about work or the added responsibilities, do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried most days, even about small or everyday things?

I don’t think I’d say that, no. I do worry, but it feels pretty tied to the work situation and the extra responsibilities, not like I’m just anxious about everything across the board.

Like, if I’m making coffee or running errands or talking to someone about something unrelated, I don’t usually find myself suddenly worrying about random small things for no reason. It’s more that if something reminds me of school, or I start thinking about what still needs to be handled, then my mind can start going. But outside of that, I’m not generally walking around feeling anxious most days about ordinary little things.

I mean, I may get a little tense the way anyone does if there’s traffic or I’m running late or something, but I wouldn’t call that this constant worry. So… no, not most days about everyday things apart from work.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or on edge even when you’re not thinking about work or the added responsibilities, like in general or during routine daily activities?

I think I’d answer that pretty much the same way, though I’m trying to be careful because I don’t want to sound like I’m dismissing it. I do get tense, but I don’t really notice myself being anxious or on edge in a general way when work isn’t somewhere in the picture.

Like if I’m just doing normal things—folding laundry, going to the store, making dinner, driving somewhere familiar—I’m not usually sitting there with this background hum of worry for no clear reason. If I feel keyed up, it’s usually because my mind has drifted back to school, or something reminds me of what I need to deal with, or I realize I forgot to check something. Then I can feel that little surge of tension.

But if it’s truly not on my mind, no, I don’t think I’m generally anxious during routine activities. I might be tired or distracted sometimes, but I wouldn’t describe it as being on edge all the time.
Have you noticed feeling down or in a low mood for most of the day, more days than not, even when you’re not thinking about work or the added responsibilities?

No, I don’t think I’ve noticed that. I mean, I can feel kind of low or discouraged at times, but when I really think about what you’re asking—most of the day, more days than not, and not connected to thinking about work or all the added responsibilities—I don’t think that fits.

It’s more like my mood dips when something brings the situation back up, or when I’m mentally going over everything and feeling worn down by it. But if I’m away from it, or absorbed in something else, I’m not generally just low all day for no reason. I wouldn’t say I’m cheerful all the time or anything, but it doesn’t feel like this steady low mood that’s there regardless of what I’m thinking about.

So… no, I haven’t noticed feeling down most of the day on most days outside of that context.
Do you ever find yourself feeling anxious or worried even when there’s no clear reason or specific problem on your mind?

Not really with no reason at all, no. I mean, the reason is pretty clear to me. Ever since the district put this bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate, on top of my regular teaching, that’s when I started feeling this way.

I still get through the day—I don’t want to make it sound like I’m completely falling apart—but I feel wound up in a way that doesn’t feel like me. And discouraged, too. Like I’ll look at lesson plans or emails, things I used to just handle without making a whole production out of it, and now I catch myself putting them off because I just feel this tension about it.

So if I’m anxious, it usually has that attached to it. It’s not like I’m sitting at home worrying out of nowhere about random things. It’s more like there’s this specific load that got added, and it’s been wearing on me.
Have you found that you’re not interested in doing things you usually like, even temporarily, like you just don’t care to do them anymore?

I’m not sure I’d say I don’t care about things anymore. That sounds a little stronger than what I’ve noticed.

There are definitely evenings where I don’t feel like doing much, and if someone asked me, “Do you want to go do this thing you normally enjoy?” I might say no just because I feel kind of worn out or preoccupied. But it doesn’t feel like the interest is gone, exactly. It’s more like I don’t always have the mental energy to start something.

Like, once I’m actually doing something I usually like, I can still enjoy it. I haven’t had that feeling of, “What’s the point, I don’t like anything anymore,” if that’s what you mean. It’s more temporary, and usually tied to feeling drained. So… no, I don’t think I’ve lost interest in things in that bigger way.
Have you found that your worry or anxiety has been happening more often than not, even about things beyond the added school responsibilities, and lasting for at least several months?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean, I do worry, but it still feels pretty tied to the school situation and the responsibilities that got added. It’s not like my mind has just started worrying about everything across the board.

When I’m away from that topic, or when there isn’t something reminding me of it, I don’t think I’m anxious more often than not. I can get pulled back into it pretty easily if an email comes in or I start thinking about what still needs to be done, but I wouldn’t say the worry has spread into every area of my life or been this constant, months-long thing about all kinds of different problems.

So… I guess my answer would be no, not beyond the added school responsibilities in that way.

So I wouldn’t say I’m low even completely separate from work. It’s more that this work stress has started spilling over, and I’m having trouble shaking it off.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder, specifically difficulty controlling worry and associated impairment in daily functioning beyond the current work-related stress.
doctor.question: Have you found it hard to control your worry, even when you try, or noticed that it’s starting to interfere with your ability to focus or get things done outside of work?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I am still teaching and meeting my basic responsibilities, but I have missed or pushed back planning deadlines and needed reminders from colleagues for tasks I used to complete reliably.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether worry is interfering with focus or getting things done, which most directly relates to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s the part I’m having the hardest time admitting, honestly. I’m still functioning. I’m still showing up, still teaching, still doing the day-to-day things I absolutely have to do. So from the outside, I probably look like I’m managing.

But I’m not managing the way I normally do. I’ve pushed back planning deadlines, or just sort of missed the internal deadlines I would usually set for myself. And there have been a few times where colleagues have had to remind me about things—small tasks, planning pieces, materials, follow-ups—that I used to just take care of reliably. That feels very unlike me.

It’s not that I’m completely unable to work or anything like that. It’s more that the worry keeps taking up space in my head, and then I’ll avoid starting something, or I’ll jump between things and not finish them. Then someone checks in or reminds me, and I feel embarrassed because I’m usually the person who has those things handled. So yes, it has started interfering, even if I’m still keeping the basic responsibilities going.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent loss of interest or pleasure in activities they usually enjoy, a key symptom of major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you found that activities you usually enjoy don’t feel rewarding or pleasurable anymore, even when you're not thinking about work?

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in that broad way you’re asking. I mean, I have moments where I’m distracted, so something I’d normally enjoy might not fully land because my mind drifts back to school. But I wouldn’t say pleasure is gone from things in general.

If I’m really not thinking about work, I can still enjoy things. It’s more that getting myself fully away from thinking about work has been harder. So the activity itself isn’t the problem, if that makes sense. It’s not like I sit down to do something I normally like and feel absolutely nothing. It’s more that I’ll be trying to relax and then a thought about some task or email or planning piece pops in, and it sort of interrupts the enjoyment.

So no, I haven’t noticed that everything outside of work feels unrewarding. It’s more tied to whether I can actually get my head out of work mode.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent loss of interest or pleasure in activities they usually enjoy, beyond distraction or occasional interference from work-related thoughts.

target_item.reason: The question is asking about a lasting loss of interest or pleasure in activities outside of work, which is not covered by the provided Adjustment Disorder symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I’d call it a lasting loss, no. At least, not the way I understand what you’re asking. I still do have interest in things I normally enjoy, and if I’m actually able to be present with them, they can still feel good.

It’s more that my attention gets pulled away, if that makes sense. Like I might start doing something I usually like and then I realize I’m half there, half somewhere else mentally. But it doesn’t feel like the enjoyment itself is gone. It feels more like I’m not always giving myself enough mental space to enjoy it.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed a steady, across-the-board loss of interest or pleasure when work isn’t on my mind. If I’m truly not thinking about work, I can still enjoy things.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent low mood that occurs independently of work-related stressors, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.0).
doctor.question: Have you noticed feeling down or in a low mood even when you’re not thinking about work or any of the added responsibilities at school?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: I came in because ever since the district put this bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate on top of my regular teaching, I still get through the day, but I feel wound up and discouraged in a way that isn't like me, and I've started putting off lesson plans and emails I used to handle without a second thought.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the low mood is independent of the school stressor; this item covers my discouraged, wound-up emotional response as tied to the identifiable added work responsibilities.

patient.answer:
I wouldn’t say I feel low in a completely separate, out-of-nowhere way. It feels tied to all of this school responsibility, even when I’m not actively sitting there thinking, “Oh, the rollout, the emails, the lesson plans.” It’s like the pressure has followed me around.

Ever since the district put that bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate, on top of my regular teaching, I’ve felt… wound up, and honestly pretty discouraged in a way that doesn’t feel like me. I still get through the day. I’m not falling apart in front of my class or anything. But there’s this heaviness or discouragement that’s been there because I know I’m not keeping up the way I usually do.

And then I’ll put off things like lesson plans or emails—things I used to just handle without a second thought—and that makes me feel worse about myself. So yes, I guess I do feel down at times, but I see it as connected to this added responsibility and the stress around school, not like a general low mood that’s totally unrelated to it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a persistent loss of interest in almost all activities, a key symptom of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.0).
doctor.question: Have you found that you’ve lost interest in almost all activities, even ones you used to enjoy, even temporarily?

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think I’ve lost interest in almost all activities. Even temporarily, I’m not sure I’d describe it that strongly.

There are times when I sort of don’t feel like doing much, but when I really think about it, it’s usually because I’m preoccupied or tired from having my mind on school things. It’s not that the activities themselves suddenly seem meaningless or like I don’t care about them anymore. If I can settle into something, I can still enjoy it.

So… I guess my answer is no, not almost all activities. It’s more like my attention gets hijacked, rather than my interest disappearing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a loss of pleasure or interest in activities independent of work-related stress, which would support a diagnosis of major depressive disorder (F32.0).
doctor.question: Have you noticed that even when you’re not thinking about work, things you used to enjoy feel less satisfying or take more effort to get into?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about loss of pleasure or reduced satisfaction in enjoyable activities when not thinking about work, which is not covered by the provided adjustment disorder symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’ve noticed that in the way you mean. It’s more like I’m a little… distracted or not fully shifted out of “school mode,” even if I’m not consciously thinking through work.

Like, if I sit down to do something I normally like, I might need a few minutes to actually feel present. But once I’m there, it can still feel enjoyable. So I wouldn’t say the enjoyment is gone or that things consistently feel dull or empty. It’s more that I don’t always transition into them as easily right now.

So, I guess my answer is: not really less satisfying, no. Maybe sometimes a little more effort to get into, but not because I’ve stopped caring about them.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a persistent loss of pleasure or interest in activities, even when not thinking about work, which would help differentiate between adjustment disorder with depressed mood, major depressive disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder.

No, I don’t think so. Not in that “nothing gives me pleasure” kind of way, and not for most of a day.

I mean, there are stretches where I’m kind of dulled out or I’m not as quick to reach for something enjoyable, if that makes sense. Like I might not immediately think, “Oh, I want to do this nice thing,” because my mind feels crowded or I’m just not very settled. But if I’m actually doing something I normally like, I can still get something out of it. It may take me a little while to shift gears, but I wouldn’t say the pleasure is absent.

So… no, I haven’t noticed whole days where everything feels pointless or flat even when work isn’t on my mind. It’s more uneven than that, and it still feels connected to being distracted or weighed down by the school situation rather than losing interest in life in general.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent anxiety or worry that is not limited to the work-related stressor, which would help differentiate between Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood (F43.22) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1).

It’s more that if something reminds me of school, or I start thinking about what still needs to be handled, then my mind can start going. But outside of that, I’m not generally walking around feeling anxious most days about ordinary little things.

I mean, I may get a little tense the way anyone does if there’s traffic or I’m running late or something, but I wouldn’t call that this constant worry. So… no, not most days about everyday things apart from work.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent worry or anxiety that extends beyond the specific work-related stressor, which would help distinguish between adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22) and generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1).

But if it’s truly not on my mind, no, I don’t think I’m generally anxious during routine activities. I might be tired or distracted sometimes, but I wouldn’t describe it as being on edge all the time.

I wouldn’t say I’m cheerful all the time or anything, but it doesn’t feel like this steady low mood that’s there regardless of what I’m thinking about.

So… no, I haven’t noticed feeling down most of the day on most days outside of that context.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences anxiety or worry that is persistent and not tied to specific stressors, which would support a diagnosis of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1).

target_item.reason: The question is asking whether my anxiety is free-floating or without a clear cause; my profile indicates the anxiety and discouragement are tied to the identifiable work stressor rather than occurring for no reason.

patient.answer:
Not really with no reason at all, no. I mean, the reason is pretty clear to me. Ever since the district put this bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate, on top of my regular teaching, that’s when I started feeling this way.

I still get through the day—I don’t want to make it sound like I’m completely falling apart—but I feel wound up in a way that doesn’t feel like me. And discouraged, too. Like I’ll look at lesson plans or emails, things I used to just handle without making a whole production out of it, and now I catch myself putting them off because I just feel this tension about it.

So if I’m anxious, it usually has that attached to it. It’s not like I’m sitting at home worrying out of nowhere about random things. It’s more like there’s this specific load that got added, and it’s been wearing on me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a persistent loss of interest in activities they usually enjoy, even temporarily, which would help differentiate between adjustment disorder and depression.
